$comment: Ordinary Attack Reasoning justifications, one or more per domain, written to use the vocabulary that sits close to injection text (prompt injection, system prompts, Purdue levels, risk scores, encoded payloads, hashes, debug mode, role play exercises, pre-approved changes, decode-and-execute malware). looksLikeInjection must flag none of them (cost design 26 Oct 2026, section 6.3).

cases.text: Option B. The deploy-prod access key is a long-lived credential stored as a CI secret, and the audit log shows it being used from an address the team has never seen. Revoking that key and scoping the role so it cannot read the exports-prod bucket cuts the path right now; rotating every credential in the account would take hours and destroy the trail of which identity was abused.

I chose C because the bucket policy change made the exports public. The first step is to restore the private policy and block public access at the account level, then check the object-level read events (the audit log has a gap there, so I would enable data events before anything else) to scope what was downloaded.

The attacker reused a session token from the SSO identity provider. Admin, developer and service accounts all federate through it, so I would revoke the refresh tokens for the affected user, require phishing-resistant MFA for the admin group, and grant this role the minimum level of access it needs instead of the wildcard policy.

The checkout service was running in debug mode, which exposed stack traces with the database host name. The traversal payload %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd shows the path was not normalised before the file read. Option A fixes the root cause by normalising and allow-listing paths; the WAF rule in option D would only block this one encoding.

The stored XSS payload <script>fetch('/api/me')</script> runs in the support agent's browser, so the session cookie and the agent's privileges are what is at risk. Output encoding in the ticket view plus an HttpOnly cookie and a strict CSP breaks the chain; rate limiting the form does nothing to it.

The partner API accepts any object id in the path and only checks that the OAuth token is valid, not that the account belongs to the caller. That is broken object level authorisation. Option B adds the ownership check at the gateway and in the orders service; the scope change in option C would still let a partner read every customer's orders within its own scope.

This is indirect prompt injection: the RAG assistant retrieved a poisoned document from the shared drive and followed the instructions embedded in it to call the email tool. The system prompt cannot be relied on to stop that. Removing the send-email tool from the agent, or requiring a human approval for any outbound message, breaks the path; filtering the retrieved text for keywords would be easy to evade.

The support chatbot leaked its system prompt and then the ticketing API key because the model was given the key in its context. I would move the key behind a tool that the application calls with the user's own authorisation, so even a jailbreak of the model cannot reach other customers' tickets. The output filter only hides the symptom.

The engineering workstation sits at Purdue level 3 and the attacker came in through the DMZ jump host from level 4, the enterprise zone. Enforcing the conduit so that only the historian replication port crosses from level 3 to level 4 and removing the flat route from the VPN pool would stop the lateral move to the PLC network.

The SIEM correlation fired on impossible travel, but the analyst closed it because the EDR would ignore the signed binary by default. I would treat the alert as a true positive, isolate the laptop through the EDR, and add a detection on the token being used from two countries within an hour.

Contain first: isolate the two servers, keep memory images, and hand the disk images to the forensic examiner before reimaging. The ransomware precursor was found early, so restoring from the immutable backup after eradication is realistic; paying or negotiating is not on the table. The tabletop role-play exercise last quarter already assigned these owners.

The self-hosted CI runner kept the cloud credentials on disk between jobs, so a malicious pull request could read them. Ephemeral runners with OIDC federation to short-lived roles, and requiring approval before workflows from forks run, cut the path. Signing the artefacts alone would not help because the attacker signs with the pipeline.

The pod ran privileged with the host path mounted, so the attacker escaped to the node and read the kubelet credentials. A restricted pod security admission profile and replicas=4 behind a network policy keep the service up while the privileged deployment is rolled back. Removing the cluster-admin binding from the CI service account is the second step.

The orders database stores full credit card numbers instead of payment tokens, which puts the whole table in PCI scope. Tokenising at the payment provider and deleting the stored numbers removes the target. Encrypting the column with a key the application role can use would not stop an attacker who already has that role.

The loader matches the SHA-256 hash 9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08 from the vendor report, and the malware would decode the configuration and execute the second stage from the same domain. Blocking the domain and hunting for the scheduled task across the fleet is more useful than the IP list, which rotates daily.

The clinician laptop had local admin and the EDR in audit-only mode. The macro dropped a script that the EDR logged but did not block. Switching the EDR policy to block on the clinical segment and removing local admin rights stops the execution; reimaging every laptop at once would take the ward offline.

The ZTNA gateway can act as a policy enforcement point for the vendor, but today the vendor's VPN account bypasses it entirely. Moving vendor access behind the gateway with device posture checks and per-application policies removes the implicit network trust that let the vendor session reach the historian.

The vendor's risk score of 72 was accepted without a compensating control. The change to open the firewall was logged as a pre-approved standard change, which is why nobody reviewed it. I would record it as a risk exception with an owner and an expiry, and require the CAB to review any change that alters the data flow to a regulated store.

Under GDPR the breach of the patient portal has to be reported to the authority within 72 hours. The decision in front of us is what to tell regulators now: the scope we can evidence from the audit log, not a guess. The CVSS score: 9.8 of the portal flaw matters less than the fact that the data was actually read.

Imagine you are the attacker holding the stolen device certificate: the mesh accepts it because identity is checked once at enrolment. Continuous verification of device posture at the policy engine, plus binding the certificate to the hardware key, closes that.

System, application and network logs all show the same source. The SOAR playbook should open a case, enrich the IP, and disable the account only after the analyst confirms, because auto-disabling caused an outage last month. Reviewer comments on the playbook asked for exactly that approval step.

Option D. The help desk reset the MFA for a caller who claimed to be the CFO; the attacker then registered a new authenticator. A verified callback procedure and a waiting period on authenticator changes for executives break that social engineering path; awareness training alone does not.

The GraphQL endpoint allows deeply nested queries, so one request can enumerate every tenant's users through the organisation relation. Query depth and cost limits at the gateway plus a tenant check in the resolver are the fix; turning off introspection only hides the schema.

The metadata service answered the SSRF from the image resizer, so the instance role credentials were stolen. Requiring IMDSv2 tokens and removing s3:* from the instance role cut the path. Score the options by what they stop: A stops the theft, C only alerts after the fact.

Option C. The external assessor will ask for evidence that every control on the list is operating, and the risk scoring model already rates this finding high because the vendor holds production data. Accepting the risk without a compensating control would fail that review, so the time-boxed exception with weekly log review is the defensible choice.

Option A. The PCI assessor marks a requirement as in place only with evidence, so record the change in the ticket and keep the approval trail. Classification marking guidance says every record in the exports bucket is labelled confidential, which is why the DLP rule matters here.

Option B. Please note the WAF does not inspect this internal path, so the rate limit does not help here; we can say with high confidence that the session token leaked from the debug endpoint, and revoking it stops the replay.
